what_its_for: Natalizumab-sztn is used to treat relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (MS) — including relapsing-remitting MS — to help reduce flare-ups (relapses) and slow the buildup of disability. It is also used to treat moderate to severe Crohn's disease in adults when other treatments have not worked well enough.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion — meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle. A healthcare provider will give you this infusion at a clinic, infusion center, or hospital. Each infusion takes about 1 hour. You will be watched by your healthcare team for at least 1 hour after each infusion to make sure you do not have a reaction. You should NOT try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: The usual dose is 300 mg given once every 4 weeks (about once a month) as an IV infusion. Your doctor will decide the exact schedule that is right for you. Do not skip or delay doses without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to go more than 4 weeks between doses. If you have missed a dose by accident, do not try to double up or take two doses at once. Your doctor will tell you when to restart your schedule.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by your healthcare provider or pharmacist at the infusion center. It is kept refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should not be frozen. The prepared infusion solution should be used within 8 hours. You do not need to store this medicine at home.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick with infections, as this medicine can weaken your immune system and make it harder to fight infections. Do not receive live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, or yellow fever vaccines) while using this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid using other medicines that weaken the immune system (such as chemotherapy or long-term steroids) along with this medicine unless your doctor specifically tells you to. Tell all of your doctors and dentists that you are receiving this medicine before any procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: confusion, memory problems, difficulty thinking clearly, or weakness on one side of your body — these could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection called PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy). Also call your doctor if you notice: signs of an allergic reaction during or after the infusion such as hives, itching, dizziness, chest pain, or trouble breathing; signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, or painful urination; unusual tiredness or weakness; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); or any new or worsening symptoms of your condition.
when_it_works: Natalizumab-sztn may start to reduce MS relapses within a few weeks to months after starting treatment, but the full benefit is usually seen after several months of regular infusions. For Crohn's disease, you may notice improvement in symptoms within 8 to 12 weeks. Because this medicine works slowly over time, it is important to keep all of your scheduled infusion appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine may affect your unborn baby or infant. A registry exists to monitor outcomes in pregnant patients — ask your doctor about it. Children: This medicine is approved for adults and is not typically used in children. Older adults: Older adults may use this medicine, but should be monitored closely by their doctor. Liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver disease, as this medicine can affect liver function. JC virus antibody testing: Your doctor will likely test you for antibodies to a virus called JC virus before and during treatment, because having this virus increases the risk of the serious brain infection PML.
